newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban lose ground in flank attack.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban lose ground in flank attack.

text.p: Forces of former Afghan military chief Ahmad Shah Masood made a flanking attack on Taleban positions north of Kabul on Wednesday bringing them to a point 13 km (eight miles) from the capital, reliable sources said.

They said Masood struck in the afternoon, pushing down the western side of the valley that runs into Kabul in an apparently successful bid to get behind the lines of the purist Islamic militiamen defending the city they took a month ago.
Separately, a Taleban spokesman in the western city of Herat implicitly admitted the militia had lost ground in what he described as heavy fighting in the remote northeastern province of Badghis.

He told the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) that Taleban fighters had killed nine men loyal to Masood's ally, northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum, and captured 70 in heavy overnight fighting in the province.
Three says ago, the Taleban said in Kabul they had captured Bagdhis and had pushed on into the neighbouring province of Faryab and were driving on its capital of Maimana.
The capture of that city would allow the Taleban to threaten Dostum's capital of Mazar-i-Sharif.
But the sources in Kabul said on Tuesday that Dostum had sent 2,000 men under General Malik, who uses only one name, to counter the Taleban thrust on the new front.

The sources, who have contacts in the area, said Malik had pushed the Taleban back into Bagdhis, which borders Turkmenistan, and by Monday there was fighting near the provincial capital of Qalaye-i-Naw.

They said the Masood attack north of Kabul was probably not aimed at the capital but at getting behnnd Taleban lines in a series of hills running part way across the valley between 25 and 30 km (15 and 20 miles) from the city.
The front lines have been static there for a week. Repeated bids by the combined forces of Masood and Dostum to break through the hills on the east side of the valley were repulsed.
Acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi said on Tuesday the latest attempt by the northern alliance to break the Taleban lines the previous night had been driven back with heavy losses.
He said 150 alliance fighters were killed and 400 wounded. There was no independent confirmation of the figures.

The sources said Masood's attack down the western side of the valley, where most villages have been abandoned in fear of fighting spreading there, could force the Taleban to weaken their defences on the eastern side.

They said it was not clear how many fighter the Taleban had available in Kabul to reinforce the front line and men might have to be drawn from elsewhere in the valley to prevent Masood getting behind them.
There are hundreds of Taleban in Kabul, mostly on security duties, but there were no signs on Wednesday afternoon of large groups leaving for the northern front.
In the northwest, it was not clear what Dostum's intentions were, the sources said.
But they said if Dostum, who controls six of Afghanistan's 33 provinces and has the country's single most powerful fighting force, could take Bagdhis, then he could threaten Herat.

The capture of that city, which has a large population of Tajiks who are cousins to Masood's people, would put Dostum's forces on the southern plains and in a position to threaten the city of Kandahar, where the Taleban have their headquarters, the sources said.
